w: The single best panorama of Florence belongs to this square across the Arno — the whole red-roofed skyline, Duomo and all, laid out below like a postcard of itself. Come for sunset, expect company: everyone else in the Oltrarno district has the same idea.
s: Florence's whole skyline, laid out below you
_facts: Square with a panoramic view of Florence
Located in the Oltrarno district

w: This hillside borgo northeast of Florence produced three major Renaissance sculptors, Desiderio da Settignano and the Rossellino brothers, thanks to the marble quarries on its doorstep — and young Michelangelo lived here with a stonemason's family. Mark Twain later rented a villa here and drafted Pudd'nhead Wilson.
s: The hill village that trained Michelangelo's eye
_facts: Hillside frazione northeast of Florence
Birthplace of sculptors Desiderio da Settignano and the Rossellino brothers, thanks to local marble quarries
Young Michelangelo lived there with a sculptor's family whose father owned a marble quarry
Mark Twain stayed at the Villa Viviani, Sept 1892 - June 1893, writing a first draft of Pudd'nhead Wilson

w: Tucked into the hills above Florence, this patrician villa is one of the Medici family's country retreats — and part of a set important enough to have been named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Medici Villas and Gardens of Tuscany. Quiet compared to the family's city palazzos, but every bit as loaded with history.
s: A UNESCO-listed Medici retreat in the hills
_facts: Patrician villa in the hills near Florence, Tuscany
Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Medici Villas and Gardens in Tuscany'

w: Moorish-Revival domes meet Italian brickwork on Via Farini, where Florence's Orthodox Jewish congregation built one of the largest synagogues in south-central Europe, completed in 1882 in the age of Jewish emancipation. It shares its building today with the city's Jewish Museum.
s: A Moorish-domed synagogue and museum in one
_facts: Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue on Via Luigi Carlo Farini
Italian and Moorish Revival styles, completed 1882
One of the largest synagogues in south-central Europe
Built in the age of Jewish emancipation reached by Tuscany's community in 1848
The Jewish Museum of Florence is located inside the synagogue

w: Inside the Palazzo Medici Riccardi, this library still keeps its books on the very shelves built to hold them — gilded, carved, late-seventeenth-century cases that have never left the room. The Riccardi family's private collection, still shelved exactly where they put it, open to the public today.
s: A private library, still on its original shelves
_facts: Public library inside the Palazzo Medici Riccardi, under the Ministry of Culture
Preserves books collected by the Riccardi family, displayed in the original rooms
Features late-17th-century carved and gilded bookshelves, largely intact

w: This medieval-turned-Renaissance palace now houses the Museum of the Old Florentine House, its rooms fitted out to show exactly how a wealthy Florentine merchant family would have lived centuries ago — furniture, frescoes, kitchen and all, rather than art on bare walls.
s: A palace museum built to look lived-in
_facts: Palace in Florence, Italy
Houses the Museum of the Old Florentine House

w: This square sits on Florence's old Roman forum, then its Jewish ghetto — both swept away in the nineteenth-century Risanamento that carved out today's grand piazza. Its Giubbe Rosse cafe became a meeting place for Futurist artists and writers, a literary coda to a site with three histories stacked up.
s: Roman forum, ghetto, then Futurist cafe society
_facts: Originally the site of Florence's Roman forum
Later the site of the city's old Jewish ghetto, cleared during the Risanamento
The Risanamento also created the city's avenues and boulevards
The square's Giubbe Rosse cafe was a meeting place for artists and writers, notably the Futurists

w: It began life in 1862 as an open-air amphitheatre seating 6,000, opening with Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor. A fire closed it down; it reopened in 1864, gained a roof in 1882, and had electricity and heating by 1911 — a venue that kept rebuilding itself into the twentieth century.
s: An open-air amphitheatre that kept reinventing itself
_facts: Opera house, originally built as the open-air Politeama Fiorentino Vittorio Emanuele amphitheatre
Inaugurated 17 May 1862 with Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor, seated 6,000
Closed by fire, reopened April 1864, gained a roof in 1882
Had electricity and heating by 1911

w: Domenico Ghirlandaio considered this his masterwork: a fresco cycle telling the life of St Francis, painted onto the walls of a chapel inside the basilica of Santa Trinita. Easy to walk past the church entirely — the frescoes reward anyone who steps inside and looks up.
s: Ghirlandaio's masterwork, hiding inside a basilica
_facts: Chapel in the basilica of Santa Trinita, Florence
Notable for frescoes of the Stories of St Francis
Considered Domenico Ghirlandaio's masterwork

w: One of the Medici family's villas in Castello, La Petraia is known for its nineteenth-century belvedere — a terrace built on axis so the view lines up perfectly with Florence spread out below. A quieter, gardened counterpart to the family's city palaces.
s: A Medici villa with a view built to order
_facts: One of the Medici villas in Castello, Florence, Tuscany
Has a distinctive 19th-century belvedere on the upper east terrace, aligned with the view of Florence
